transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-26 15:00 UTC | Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Alice Nguyen (Redwood AE), Samir Das (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, Borealis), Maya Lin (ML Eng), Evan Ortiz (PM), Leila Hassan (Security)

[00:00] Alice (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:04] Raj (CTO): Raj here.
[00:05] Maya: Maya - hi.
[00:06] Evan: Evan here.
[00:07] Leila: Leila here.
[00:08] Alice: Great. Samir and Jordan from our engineering team are on to cover integration and benchmarks.

[00:28] Samir (SE): Cool, I'll kick off with our typical POC framework. We want to confirm success criteria, workload shape, and integration surface—SDK, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and function/tool calling. Quick question on success criteria from your side?
[00:38] Evan (PM): For product, primary success is 95% of classification outputs matching our current rule-based labels within the POC test set, and response latency under 300ms for short prompts. Cost target is also important - we need to see at least 40% TCO improvement vs our current inference fleet.
[00:56] Raj (CTO): To add, operationally we need predictable tail latency — p95 under 600ms, preferably under 500ms. And we cannot send any PHI outside our VPC for the POC, so private deployment or VPC peering is required.
[01:15] Leila (Security): Also SOC2 compliance and KMS-managed keys, audit logs for inference requests, and RBAC for who can call the API. We'll need those before any production rollout.

[01:40] Jordan (SE): Noted. On VPC we offer a private deployment option and VPC peering for dedicated clusters; we also have a hosted option with encryption at rest and in transit. For the POC we can do a private VPC peering or a dedicated cluster in a Redwood-managed account depending on which you prefer.
[01:58] Raj: We prefer VPC peering if possible — keeps control on our side.

[02:10] Samir: Great. On workload sizing — you mentioned average QPS?
[02:15] Maya: Current traffic for the features we're targeting is about 20 qps average and spikes up to ~200 qps during batch runs. Typical prompt lengths are short — 30 to 80 tokens per request — but we also have a smaller set of longer-context queries for rerankers at ~1k tokens.
[02:32] Samir: That helps. For 20 qps avg with 200 peak, we'll provision a pool and run autoscale policies. For low-latency short prompts we recommend a low-seq optimized model, potentially a quantized variant to keep cost down. That also plays into our OpenAI-compatible endpoints — you can switch between model variants via the same API path.
[02:52] Evan: Is function calling supported in the OpenAI-compatible layer? We have some tools that need structured JSON outputs.
[02:58] Jordan: Yes, our API supports function/tool calling and structured output. It mirrors the OpenAI semantics — you can declare function signatures, and the model will return JSON-like outputs. One caveat: in some edge cases our transcriber shows slight naming issues, so we calibrate the schema validation in post-processing — it's pretty standard.

[03:20] Maya: That's good. We also use an internal SDK in Python and TypeScript. What's the integration work like?
[03:25] Samir: SDKs are straightforward — we have official SDKs for JS and Python, and the OpenAI-compatible endpoints mean minimal code changes. You can switch the base URL to Redwood, and the parameters are mostly identical. For streaming and function calling we have examples in our repo; we'll share a snippet.
[03:45] Alice (AE): We'll attach a sample repo link in the follow-up.

[03:55] Raj: On benchmarks, we'd like to run perf tests with our prompt set and measure latency, cost per 1k tokens, and accuracy vs baseline. How long does Redwood need to run a benchmark?
[04:06] Samir: For a representative run, 2 hours with steady-state traffic is typical, plus another 4 hours for longer-context/throughput tests. We'll need your sample prompts and token distribution; if you can provide 1M prompts or a smaller stratified sample that's fine.
[04:22] Maya: We can produce a stratified 200k sample in a few days.

[04:35] Jordan: For accuracy evaluation it'd help to get your ground truth labels and an automated eval harness. We can run the model suite and output per-example diffs. We'll also run canary shifts between hosted and dedicated variants to estimate cost deltas.
[04:50] Evan: About deployment modes — quick recap of tradeoffs? Hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[04:56] Jordan: Hosted is fastest to get started, best for time-to-value. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation within Redwood, with reserved capacity pricing. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives full control for compliance but requires more setup. For your VPC peering ask, private/dedicated are likely the right choices.
[05:16] Leila: If we do VPC peering can we still have Redwood-managed KMS, or must we use our HSM?
[05:22] Samir: Both options supported — you can bring your KMS, or use Redwood's customer-managed keys in your cloud account. For HSM we have options via our enterprise package. We'll include KMS integration details in the security doc.
[05:45] Raj: Pricing - we need a rough estimate for the POC monthly cost for the dedicated pool for 20 qps baseline with 200 peak, and hosted per-call costs for fallback.
[05:56] Alice: We'll provide a pricing worksheet with modeled scenarios: dedicated reserved pool vs hosted fallbacks. Expect a preliminary back-of-envelope within 48 hours.
[06:10] Maya: How do you handle prefix caching and KV cache? We rely on session state for fast reranking.
[06:16] Jordan: We support KV cache management and prefix caching; you can pin sessions to keep caches warm for a set of users. That reduces token cost and latency substantially. Note: our transcript sometimes shows KV as kay-vee in docs, but it's the same thing.
[06:35] Evan: Any constraints on function calling and structured outputs for high throughput?
[06:40] Samir: Structured outputs are fine at scale; the main cost is tokens for the output schema. We'll recommend designs that minimize verbosity. For high-throughput function calls we can stream partial responses to reduce latency.
[07:02] Alice: Let's talk timeline — what's a reasonable POC schedule?
[07:06] Raj: We'd like a 6-week POC: week 1 discovery and environment setup, week 2 data handoff and bench harness, weeks 3-4 benchmarks + tuning, week 5 integration tests, week 6 final evaluation and business review.
[07:19] Samir: That fits our standard cadence. We can do environment setup in 3-5 business days once we have the VPC details, and run the benchmark in week 2/3.
[07:30] Leila: We'll need a legal/data processing addendum before we start sending logs — can you share the DPA and SOC2 report?
[07:36] Alice: Yes. We'll include DPA, SOC2 summary, and our security checklist in the follow-up.
[07:48] Evan: For the benchmark harness, any preferences for running it in our infra vs Redwood infra?
[07:53] Jordan: We can run the harness in your VPC (preferred for exact network conditions) or run a Redwood-managed sim. For accuracy and cost numbers it's better to run against your VPC-peered dedicated cluster.
[08:10] Maya: On model variants: do you suggest off-the-shelf open models or Redwood-verified tuned variants?
[08:17] Samir: We'll propose a small set: a low-latency quantized variant for short prompts, a base variant for accuracy comparisons, and a long-context variant for reranking. The POC will benchmark all three.
[08:35] Raj: Any blockers you foresee?
[08:38] Samir: Mostly data handoff and network setup for VPC peering. Also KMS/HSM choices can add lead time. We'll flag those in the POC doc.
[08:52] Alice: Next steps recap — we'll send the POC scope doc, pricing worksheet, security pack, and sample SDK snippets. Samir will prepare benchmark harness and propose dates.
[09:05] Raj: Sounds good. One small question — do you support audit logs per token/call for our compliance feed?
[09:11] Jordan: Yes, we can stream audit logs to your log sink; retention policies are configurable. We'll include retention and log schema in the security doc.
[09:25] Maya: Any specific sample code for function calling in TypeScript?
[09:29] Jordan: Yes, we'll attach a TypeScript snippet showing function signatures and structured output parsing.
[09:36] Alice: Perfect. Anything else from the Borealis side?
[09:40] Leila: Just to reiterate, encryption key ownership and proof of SOC2 are hard blockers for our security sign-off.
[09:46] Alice: Understood — we'll make those priority attachments.
[09:55] Evan: Great, thanks everyone.
[09:58] Alice: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the documents and a proposed bench run slot by end of week.
[10:04] Raj: Thanks.

End of call.
